summary: 15Mn5Ni is a Ni-bearing, lower-Mn austenitic low-density steel of nominal composition Fe–15Mn–9Al–0.9C–5Ni (wt.%). It was produced by vacuum induction melting, homogenized at 1423 K for 2.5 h, hot rolled at 1323 K (HR), cold rolled at room temperature to ~50% thickness reduction (HR+CR), and finally heat treated at 873 K for 1 h followed by water quenching. The parent study asks how the Mn/Ni ratio governs concurrent κ-carbide/B2 precipitation and austenite recrystallization, and hence the mechanical response of Fe–Mn–Al–C–(Ni) low-density steels; for this particular 873 K condition the paper reports hardness behaviour only.
composition: Nominal composition Fe–15Mn–9Al–0.9C–5Ni (wt.%), designated 15Mn5Ni. The measured chemistry (wet chemical analysis and emission spectroscopy) is Mn 14.7 ± 0.3, Al 9.8 ± 0.05, C 0.9 ± 0.01, Ni 4.1 ± 0.05, Fe balance (all in wt.%). Mn and C are austenite stabilizers and C also provides interstitial solid-solution hardening; Al is a ferrite stabilizer added mainly to lower the physical density of the steel; Ni is added because the strongly negative enthalpy of formation between Ni and Al promotes precipitation of hard Ni-rich ordered B2 Fe(Ni)Al-type intermetallic particles. Among the three alloys of the study (28Mn0Ni, 28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni), this grade combines the lowest Mn level with a Ni addition and a slightly higher Al level, giving the highest prior B2 fraction and the highest κ-carbide volume fraction.
processing: Processing route: (1) vacuum induction melting (VIM) under vacuum, producing a 30 kg ingot from which the sound portion was taken; (2) homogenization of the sound ingot at 1423 K for 2.5 h; (3) hot rolling at 1323 K to a final plate thickness of about 13 mm — this condition is designated HR; (4) cold rolling at room temperature in several passes to ~50% reduction in thickness (~6 mm thick sheets), designated HR+CR; 15Mn5Ni cracked beyond 50% cold reduction, so the reduction was deliberately limited to 50% for all three alloys to keep the comparison at a fixed degree of cold work; (5) heat treatment of the cold-rolled sheets at 873 K (within the 873–1273 K range explored in the study) for 1 h followed by water quenching. Heat-treated samples are referred to by their heat-treatment temperature, so this sample corresponds to the HR+CR+873 K condition. The hot-rolling details are reported in a companion study [21].
microstructure: In the hot-rolled (HR) precursor state the alloy consists of a γ-austenite matrix with equiaxed grains of d ≈ 5–7 μm and nearly random texture, together with an ordered BCC B2 (Fe(Ni)Al-type) phase at ~12 vol.% appearing as elongated stringers (bamboo-like morphology) and polygonal particles, plus κ-carbide precipitates; this B2 fraction is markedly higher than in the higher-Mn 28Mn5Ni alloy (~4%), and the alloy also carries the highest κ-carbide volume fraction of the three grades. Its annealing-twin fraction is lower (microstructures of the higher-Mn Ni-bearing grades contain ~28–40% twins) than in higher-Mn low-density steels. After cold rolling to 50% (the direct precursor of the 873 K condition) the austenite grains are deformed and exhibit parallel planar slip bands, with no evidence of deformation twinning or martensitic transformation; the prior B2 stringers deform concurrently with the austenite, their average thickness decreasing from ~8 μm to ~2 μm before being sheared and fragmented at ~35–45° to the rolling direction, with stringers in near <100> orientation. In the heat-treated states of the parent study, three features coexist — deformed austenite, recrystallized austenite with annealing twins, and secondary B2 (fine intragranular 50–200 nm and coarser intergranular 0.5–1.5 μm). The 873 K condition of this specific sample is, however, documented for hardness only; no EBSD/TEM microstructural description is reported for it, and the microstructural information above pertains to the HR and HR+CR states of the same alloy.
properties: Hardness (Vickers, ~300 N peak load, 15 s dwell, ASTM E-140-02, averaged over ten measurements) is the property reported for this 873 K condition. In the HR state the alloy has the highest hardness of the three grades, ~375 ± 6 VHN (versus ~256 ± 5 VHN for 28Mn0Ni and ~268 ± 5 VHN for 28Mn5Ni). Hardness increases with cold reduction and saturates at around 450 VHN at 50% thickness reduction, where 15Mn5Ni is ~20 VHN harder than 28Mn0Ni. Upon subsequent heat treatment at 873 K the hardness of the Ni-containing alloys (28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni) rises to 500 VHN, whereas the Ni-free 28Mn0Ni shows no noticeable change; under any given heat treatment the Ni-containing alloys remain significantly harder than 28Mn0Ni. Tensile results for this alloy in the 873 K condition are not reported (the study notes that tensile properties at 973 K and 1023 K are unavailable because the alloy fails in a brittle manner with <1% elongation). Characterization techniques applied in the parent study comprise OIM-EBSD (SEM, step sizes 120 and 250 nm, KAM and GOS<2° analysis, Σ3 twin fraction, linear-intercept grain size), X-ray diffraction with Co-Kα radiation, TEM/SAED with EDS (B2 composition) on twin-jet electropolished specimens, SEM fractography of failed tensile specimens, Vickers hardness and room-temperature tensile testing (ASTM E8M, gauge length 30 mm, width 6 mm, ~3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, 0.5 mm min⁻¹ cross-head speed) including interrupted tests.
mechanisms: Cold rolling to 50% → austenite accommodates strain predominantly by planar slip (parallel slip bands); no deformation twinning or martensite forms, so work hardening comes from dislocation accumulation (Taylor hardening, σ ∝ ρ^1/2) rather than transformation-induced plasticity.

Cold rolling → the ordered B2 stringers share load with the austenite and undergo concurrent progressive microstructural change (dislocation accumulation, substructure development, thickness reduction from ~8 μm to ~2 μm and finally shearing/fragmentation at ~35–45° to the rolling direction), showing that even an ordered intermetallic phase deforms plastically during rolling.

Ni addition + the strongly negative Ni–Al enthalpy of formation → precipitation of fine Ni-rich ordered B2 particles in the 973–1173 K range, whose concurrent formation during heat treatment delays austenite recrystallization by altering diffusion characteristics and boundary migration.

Concurrent second-phase precipitation → recrystallization is controlled in two opposite ways depending on particle size: coarse stringer B2 acts as a particle-stimulated-nucleation (PSN) site that assists recrystallization, whereas fine intragranular/intergranular B2 and κ-carbide exert a Zener-Smith drag; nucleation of recrystallized grains occurs preferentially along γ/γ boundaries and γ/B2 interfaces, and intragranular B2 does not pin new grains but retards the overall recovery process.

Heat treatment in the two-phase (γ + B2) region → reduced grain-boundary migration and mobility (lower diffusivities) → refined austenite grain structure and suppression of grain growth in the Ni-containing alloys, whereas the B2-free 28Mn0Ni undergoes pronounced grain growth at 1173 K.

Ni-rich B2 precipitation → increased carbon rejection from B2 into the neighbouring austenite → facilitates κ-carbide formation in Ni-added low-density steels; lowering Mn at a similar Ni level (as in 15Mn5Ni) has a more pronounced effect on κ-carbide coarsening than Ni addition alone.

κ-carbide formation → κ-carbides form by spinodal decomposition during quenching; they are coarse (10–60 nm) and inhomogeneous inside deformed austenite but fine and uniformly distributed within recrystallized austenite, the finer ones promoting glide-plane softening and hence a higher strain-hardening rate.

Heat treatment at 873 K after 50% cold rolling → the Ni-containing alloys harden to ~500 VHN while the Ni-free alloy does not, because Ni-rich B2 and κ-carbide precipitation adds precipitation strengthening that offsets the softening from recovery/recrystallization (which is still negligible in these alloys at 873 K).

Deformation of the heat-treated alloy → planar slip activity followed by dynamic slip band refinement, together with dislocation–twin interaction in recrystallized austenite, governs strain hardening; non-shearable B2 particles act as obstacles to dislocation motion and trigger early slip-band refinement, while coarse κ-carbides delay refinement at low strains and produce inhomogeneous slip-band spacing in Ni-containing steels.

Low-temperature heat treatment (973–1023 K) of Ni-containing lower-Mn steel → a low recrystallized fraction combined with large volume fractions of B2 (including prior stringers) and coarser grain-boundary κ-carbide/B2 precipitates → crack-initiation-controlled, fast-propagating intergranular fracture along γ/B2 interphase boundaries and quasi-cleavage failure, giving <1% tensile elongation.

Heat treatment at 1173 K → complete dissolution of κ-carbides and partial dissolution of B2 (fine intragranular and intergranular particles dissolve faster than stringers), causing a sudden rise in the recrystallized austenite fraction and restoring ductility without losing the benefit of residual B2 strengthening.
conclusions: For this alloy composition the parent study concludes that Ni addition to a lower-Mn Fe–15Mn–9Al–0.9C–5Ni austenitic low-density steel has a detrimental effect at low heat-treatment temperatures: at 873 K the alloy is the hardest of the three grades studied (hardness rising to ~500 VHN, the same level as the higher-Mn 28Mn5Ni, and clearly above the Ni-free 28Mn0Ni), and at 973–1023 K the large volume fraction of B2 (including prior stringers) together with co-precipitated coarser κ-carbides and B2 along grain boundaries makes the alloy brittle (<1% tensile elongation, quasi-cleavage/intergranular fracture along γ/B2 boundaries). Only upon heat treatment at 1173 K — with complete κ-carbide dissolution and partial B2 dissolution producing a sharp rise in the recrystallized austenite fraction — does the alloy regain ductility (YS 971 ± 5 MPa, UTS 1303 ± 12 MPa, TE 36 ± 1%, n = 0.30), matching the strength–ductility level of 28Mn5Ni with improved strain-hardening characteristics. Its processing window is therefore placed around 1173 K, in contrast to ~973 K for the Ni-free 28Mn0Ni alloy and a wider, more flexible window for 28Mn5Ni. More broadly, the study shows that processing in the two-phase region is an effective way to refine grains and that concurrent B2 precipitation has a stronger effect on recrystallization kinetics than κ-carbides, so the Mn/Ni ratio is the key variable in selecting the two-phase processing window of austenitic low-density steels.
unmapped: This specific 873 K sample is not covered by EBSD, XRD, TEM or tensile testing in the paper; the 873 K condition is documented for hardness only, so its microstructural and tensile descriptions here are drawn from the HR and HR+CR states of the same alloy and from the general behaviour of the alloy family.

TEM-EDS shows that the B2 phase is an FeAl-based ordered phase containing significant Mn and Ni; for 15Mn5Ni the B2 particles analysed after 1173 K treatment contain Mn 10.5–8.7 wt.% and Ni 20.2–22.0 wt.% with Al 12.8–13.5 wt.% (Fe balance), i.e. clearly lower Mn and Ni than the B2 in the higher-Mn 28Mn5Ni alloy.

Cold rolling of this alloy beyond 50% thickness reduction caused cracking, which is why the whole study fixed the cold reduction at 50%; the low room-temperature ductility of 15Mn5Ni in the hot-rolled condition was identified as the reason for its increased cracking tendency under heavier cold rolling.

The initial hardness values of the three grades in the HR condition (~375 ± 6 VHN for 15Mn5Ni) come from a companion study of the same authors [21], which also reported that the hot-rolled alloys reached only 20–70% total tensile elongation to failure.
